How to read every card: the bold heading is plain English · the grey sentence is the detail · the mono block is the exact file, line or statement. Read only the bold lines and the board still makes complete sense.

tools/boardgen/build_board.py draws this board from the repository
What the operator actually loads: a compiled React app that talks to exactly one address, on its own origin.
main.tsx creates a single query client and mounts the app. App.tsx owns every route, the error boundary and the suspense
fallback. No second router, no state library.
Server state lives in one cache
Every request goes through TanStack Query: fifteen-second stale time, one retry and only for 5xx, no refetch on focus. A
mutation invalidates the keys it touched, so a save and a list cannot disagree.
The whole backend contract is one file. The base URL is the literal string /api, so the browser calls the address it was already
loaded from — no hostname, no CORS rule, no per-environment variable.
ApiError means the server answered and refused. NetworkError means it never answered. The UI shows different text for each,
and the smoke suite asserts both.
Dashboard, Projects, Tasks, Clients, Partners, QA, Releases, Contracts, Insights, Activity, Workload, Settings, plus a catch-all.
useQueryState normalises loading / error / empty / data, so no page invents its own spinner or its own failure text.
Open tabs poll /api/changes and invalidate whatever changed. Not websockets, not a queue — one endpoint that answers
the same hook writes the log it reads
Vite compiles the screens to static files, and the service build turns those files into a TypeScript module so they travel inside
app.ts defines the request path; routes/index.ts holds every handler; services and domain hold the rules.
Thirteen lines are the entire lifecycle. Order is the design: the error handler sits after the hooks so it can catch their failures.
Handlers call SQL directly for reads. Services own multi-step writes and invariants. repositories/ is a mapper module, not a
repository layer. No ORM, no DI, no per-resource routers.
Ninety-four handlers in one file, grouped by domain with blank-line sections. Every route is easy to find; the file is 3,370 lines,
which is the largest single piece of debt here.
Zod at the route, before any business logic; small helpers for scalars. A failure throws badRequest with the field named.
ok() gives {data}, page() adds meta, and every error — 400/404/409/500 — is rendered by the same handler, so the client
One onRequest hook resolves the single operator row and caches it per instance. Every write is attributed to that user.
The interesting part of a table is not its columns — it is what it refuses to store. This is the DDL that actually runs.
The table that is actually created
Read the constraints as sentences: rules the application cannot bypass.
Ids and timestamps are decided in code
Ids are prefixed and time-sortable, so a row says what it is and roughly when. Timestamps are stored as "YYYY-MM-DD
HH:MM:SS" UTC — deliberately not ISO with a T, because a space sorts before a T and mixing the two silently reorders every
A client has projects; a project has boards and phases; a board has columns; a column holds tasks; a task has checks. Every
arrow is a real foreign key except the two below.
A deadline timer points at any entity (deal, project, task, release), so it is polymorphic by design. A QA report outlives the
release it tested, so it is not deleted with it.
db/postgres/schema.sql calls itself "the production system of record" and carries CHECK (length(title) >= 4). Nothing applies
it: boot migrates from db/migrations/pg, and CI never runs schema.sql. The title rule is really enforced at routes/index.ts:392
Seventeen numbered files, applied in order at boot, each recorded with a checksum in schema_migrations. A slow migration
delays every cold start; a broken one blocks it.
Four build steps and five runtime steps. Nothing compiles while a page is loading.
Build time — once per deploy, on Vercel
Dev dependencies included: the build needs vite and tsc.
Vite compiles React into static files.
Those files become one TypeScript module.
Ten reusable connections, not one per
Ensure exactly one users row exists.

Why step 3 of the build exists: Vercel bundles what is imported, not what sits in a folder — and the services schema rejects includeFiles. So the built screens are compiled into the API as a module (16 assets) instead of copied next to it.
Two journeys cover almost everything: fetching a list, and creating a record. Both are single round trips.
One request, one query. The counts are correlated subqueries, so there is no N+1, and the mapper turns snake_case into what
FROM projects p JOIN clients c ON …
Six steps, each able to stop the write with a named reason. The column is looked up by (board_id, key), never guessed; the
key comes from the highest existing suffix, not the row count.
The status is a fact about the request, not a mood. Every one arrives in the same envelope.
What the client can rely on
One parser for the whole API, because there is one error renderer.
click → rewrite → router → onRequest → identity → zod → service → column → key → insert → response hooks (log, metric,
The distinction most diagrams get wrong: a corridor with locked doors is not the same thing as a signpost.
A transition that is not in the table is refused with 409. Guarded moves require evidence rows.
dev_complete → qa_approved → lead_approved → client_accepted, unique per task and step.
A task cannot be called done while a gate rule is unsatisfied: description written, owner assigned, estimate set, and five more.
A release cannot ship while a required QA check is open. A running timer past its due date becomes missed — daily, and on
A deal can be PATCHed to any stage. There is no rule about which may follow which — the arrows on any diagram of it are
Seven allowed values in a CHECK constraint. A constraint is not a state machine: any allowed value can follow any other.
columns.wip_limit is stored and seeded, and nothing reads it. No column refuses a card because it is full.
A diagram with arrows looks enforced, and a reader will believe it. Only the left column is code that can refuse you.
An earlier version of this board
There is no queue and no worker. Reliability here means health endpoints, one honest sweep, and tests written after real failures.
Liveness and readiness are separate questions, and the answers are different on purpose.
A running timer past its due date must become missed. That is one UPDATE, so it runs wherever a process is awake: the
Vercel cron at 03:00, an interval every 60 s in the container, and a throttled inline sweep on the serverless path.
A restore drill creates a fresh database, applies a dump and reads the data back — because an untested backup is a hope, not
Story 1 · the database that was not there
An earlier revision fell back to a file database when DATABASE_URL was missing. On a serverless host that file lives in /tmp
and dies with the instance — the app booted, accepted writes, read them back, and lost them. The fix was to refuse to start
Story 2 · the outage with no route to report it
@fastify/static was imported at the top of app.ts. 10.1.4 pulled in an ESM-only dependency; on a runtime without
require(esm) that threw while the module loaded, before any route existed. Every request answered boot_failed.
fix: pin 10.1.3 + import inside the branch
There is no retry ladder and no dead-letter queue. A failed write returns its error to the client; the client decides. Nothing
What "green" means, what is actually protected, and what a new engineer should know before touching it.
One command a person runs before pushing. It stops at the first failure.
283 tests across 24 files; 19 of them run again against a real PostgreSQL 16, because SQLite and Postgres disagree about
A build can pass while the server never starts. So CI builds the way production builds, then starts the artefact and calls it.
Four tests that exist because of an outage
A child process loads the server with ESM require disabled — the runtime shape that broke in July — and asserts it still boots.
There is no authentication, and the API says so in its own response rather than leaving you to guess.
Platform password protection on the deployment, plus these application controls.
helmet · cors · 2 MB body · rate limits
project_members, partner_iam_users and client_portal_users exist, and scope.ts can restrict by membership. With one admin
operator the scope resolves to everything, so it never fires.
The router file is first, then the missing per-user identity, then the dashboard aggregates computed on every request.
If you only have ten minutes: read the map on the left, then follow the reading order on the right.
Six folders hold everything. Learn these and you can find any behaviour in the system.
services/ domain/ rules: lifecycle, gates, clocks
Every statement on this board has a command or a file behind it. In a fresh clone:
npm run verify # all ten gates
npm run test:pg # needs a real PostgreSQL
Twenty terms, each in one line, all of them used on this board.
rate limit · embedded SPA · cold start
Reading order for a new engineer
Six files, in this order, is the whole system: how it starts, how it routes, how it writes, how it migrates, how the screen calls it,
Three things could not be observed from outside the deployment, so they are asserted nowhere on this board.
